Article Title: Between parents' struggles and 'endless coffees': How Savitha Shri became India's only gold medallist at Chess Olympiad | Exclusive
Article Text:
Savitha Shri speaks about Chess Olympiad

Swayams Mishra with Savitha Shri at Samarkand Olympiad (FIDE Photo)

A reserve who ended up playing almost every round

Savitha wins an individual gold on Board 5 at Women's Chess Olympiad (Photo by Michal Walusza for FIDE)

A murky start, and the climb back from Kazakhstan and China

Savitha Shri in Round 10 of Chess Olympiad (Photo by Michal Walusza for FIDE)

The captain who brought the 'endless coffees'

Swayams Mishra at Samarkand Olympiad (FIDE Photo)

What's next?

NEW DELHI: Savitha Shri Baskar emerged as India's golden girl at the 2026 Chess Olympiad, but there was a point when her chess career was funded by her father's gold jewellery, pawned to cover a national tournament's entry fee.Baskar, an electrician in Singapore at the time, would go on to quit that job entirely and move back to India to support her daughter. It was a decision he still calls difficult.The sacrifice, in fact, wasn't only his to make. Chess had first entered the family through Savitha's older brother Mugesh, whom their father had originally set out to build a career around.Savitha's own interest came from watching him play. But once both children were training together, the costs made running two chess careers impossible. Mugesh stepped back after the eighth standard. Savitha kept going.This time, she went to Samarkand as the youngest member of the Indian contingent, brought in after Harika Dronavalli, who felt she'd achieved everything a chess career could offer , including a gold, stepped aside for the next generation.Even then, there were questions about the 19-year-old International Master's spot in the squad. "There were a lot of people who questioned her spot, journalists saying there are players higher than her, and so on," women's captain Swayams Mishra had earlier told TimesofIndia.com "But according to the selection, she was qualified, and she'd won the Asian continental a couple of months ago. She'd also played the World Women's Team Championship, so I knew her as a team player always. Whenever we gave her the opportunity, she delivered. If India won a medal, we owe it to her."Savitha delivered in some style, becoming the only Indian to win an individual gold medal in Uzbekistan, finishing an extraordinary 9/10, and a central figure in India's bronze-medal campaign."Coming to the team as a reserve player, I wasn't even expecting to play all 10 rounds," she told TimesofIndia.com during an exclusive interaction. "So I'm grateful for the trust my teammates and my captain had in me, for giving me the opportunity to play all 10. I'm happy with the score, 9 out of 10; but game-wise, I think I could have done a bit better."Around her sat some of the biggest names in Indian women's chess. Looking back at her first experience of the Olympiad, she continued, "It was my first Olympiad, and it has always been a dream for me to play for the country in a tournament like this. We had Humpy (Koneru) akka, who's been the top-most player in women's chess for almost two decades, and we had Vaishali akka and Divya Deshmukh; such a strong team, and we were the first seed in the women's section. I learned a lot from all of them, and Abhijit sir and Swayams sir did a wonderful job with our openings and in every other aspect too. It was a wonderful experience."Despite the individual gold, she's unambiguous about where her priorities sat throughout. "The team medal will always come first, because we're giving out everything for the team. I wasn't even caring about my individual gold; someone told me I'd already secured a medal before the last round, but I only found out I'd won gold after the round finished," she recalled with a laugh. "I was just trying my best to win that last game so we could get a silver as a team. From the position I got, I couldn't really convert anything, but I'm at least happy we got the bronze."The campaign didn't begin smoothly off the board. "When we arrived (in Samarkand) at the hotel, it was around 11:30 at night, and they said they couldn't get the rooms ready," Savitha told this website. "We didn't get our rooms for five or six hours. They made us wait in the lobby, then gave one or two rooms for the whole team."What followed, though, was a federation stepping up as Savitha confirmed, "After that, AICF made sure everything was sorted, and that we got our Indian food every day. The Indian restaurant was so far away that they had to arrange someone to get the delivery done, and they made sure the food was good quality and on time. I don't think any federation would have done that. We're all so grateful for it."On the board, the campaign's defining stretch came against Kazakhstan and China, the two matches where her own result decided India's fate."With both teams, I was the one playing till the last point, and my game was going to be the deciding factor," she said. "It started with Kazakhstan; I got an equal position and was trying to push it. I think what helped me score was time management: after move 40 I was always ahead on the clock compared to my opponent, which put more pressure on them, and I was able to swindle the position."Against China, the margins were just as tight. "It's a bit sad we couldn't win that one," the teenager added. "When I got a better position, Vantika made a blunder at that point and got into a worse position. If she'd been able to hold a draw, I think we'd have got gold fairly easily."Through the toughest stretches, Savitha points to one figure in particular for keeping the team together, especially after an early loss to Poland."Swayams sir is the best captain ever, I think, because of the way he handled our team. We lost to Poland, but he was the one who motivated us. Even during games, if we wanted something, he was always there: water, bananas, everything. For me, he was bringing endless coffees, because I played till the last moment every time. He even jokingly said it was because of those coffees that I was able to swing all my games." The backing went beyond logistics, she said. "He had so much confidence in me. I think he believed in me more than I believed in myself."That trust, she added, was something she'd first experienced a cycle earlier, at the Asian Games, and carried with her into Samarkand."There's just so much you learn from being in a team like that, discussing lines together in team meetings, having those interactions, and them having so much confidence in me. They believed in me more than I did in myself at the time too," she noted.Asked whether she thinks back to what her family gave up to get her here, Savitha is candid, albeit guarded, about letting it weigh on her day-to-day. "If I don't play well, it all comes back to mind. My parents struggled. I know what they've gone through, because they had to spend so much on chess because of me. That's something I'll always remember. But I don't really think much about it while I'm playing, or in general. I just have to stay in the present.Savitha, currently rated 2405, is treating the grandmaster (GM) title as a goal to work toward rather than something owed to her on reputation."The Grandmaster title is definitely my goal, and I'll be working towards it," she said in a confident voice. "I'll be playing tournaments, of course, but for now I think I'll take a bit of rest. The Olympiad is such a big and tiring event. My next tournament will probably be the World Juniors in Namibia, though I might play something before that. I haven't decided yet."On where her game itself needs to sharpen next, she concluded, "In my own game, I think I should get a bit steadier in the openings, and probably work on some positional stuff as well. In the Olympiad, I played the aggressive, complicated positions pretty well; positional chess is the other part I'll be working on."
Article Summary: Savitha Shri Baskar is the only Indian to win an individual gold medal in Uzbekistan. She was brought in after Harika Dronavalli, who felt she'd achieved everything a chess career could offer, stepped aside for the next generation. The 19-year-old International Master was a central figure in India's bronze- medal campaign.

Article Title: Khalid Jamil’s bolder India faces Uruguay as Forlan begins rebuilding after World Cup debacle
Article Text:
Image credit: Indian Football

KOLKATA: In the past few days, Diego Forlan and his Uruguay team have been staying here like passive guests, happily blending into the background and letting Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil enjoy the public eye. With the departure of their fellow South American rivals, the spotlight is back on La Celeste. So is India’s final act of their extraordinary brush with three World Cup teams in this Fifa international window.Being a football team in transition comes with its own set of challenges. In holding Panama 1-1 and even in losing 0-4 to Brazil, Khalid Jamil’s team has shown glimpses of promise. Teams under Jamil are always known for being defensively strong; sitting deep in numbers is a celebrated way of making life difficult for the opponents. A paradigm shift is now noticeable in the system. India look bolder, more ambitious.“It’s not about me and all credit goes to players,” the former India midfielder told TOI during the pre-match news conference on Monday, the eve of their clash with Uruguay at Salt Lake Stadium.Jamil, however, has warned his players of not repeating the mistakes they had committed against Brazil. “Don’t concede early,” was his advice.Uruguay have stars like Darwin Nunez, Rodrigo Bentancur, Ronald Araujo and Jose Maria in their squad with players equipped with elite mentality. Ranked 20th in the world, they are expected to come hard at the home team with their typical aggression and physicality.Forlan, Golden Ball winner of the 2010 World Cup and an icon in Uruguayan football, also is tasked with rebuilding a team whose World Cup campaigned collapsed into a player revolt against his predecessor Marcelo Bielsa.“I want my players to understand that I’m going to be the same if they win and I’m going to be the same if they lose. But the most important thing is to give your best,” Forlan said in replying to a question from the TOI.“When you win, you’re not the best and when you lose you’re not the worst,” he said.
Article Summary: India take on Uruguay in their final World Cup warm-up match. Khalid Jamil's team have shown glimpses of promise in recent matches. Uruguay have stars like Darwin Nunez, Rodrigo Bentancur, Ronald Araujo and Jose Maria.

Article Title: India 'A' pacers look to step up to the plate against Australia 'A'
Article Text:

PUDUCHERRY: In an era where 350-plus totals in ODIs are becoming the norm, fast bowlers are often left walking a tightrope. India’s recent ODI series against the West Indies was a case in point, with the bowlers conceding 295 and 405 in the first two games before West Indies chased down 352 in the final ODI with 10 balls to spare.As India look towards the 2027 World Cup, where they begin their campaign against Australia on Oct 7, the threematch one-day series between India ‘A’ and Australia ‘A’ in Puducherry offers another window into the country’s pace reserves.The big question is: who can eventually emerge as the ideal partner for Jasprit Bumrah With Arshad Khan , Gurjapneet Singh and Yash Thakur are part of the India ‘A’ setup, it will be interesting to see if anyone can step up.India ‘A’ coach Lakshmipathy Balaji believes the cupboard is far from bare. For him, the answer lies as much in patience and nurturing as it does in raw numbers.“Many have potential. High-scoring games are common now, but bowlers will adapt over time. Bumrah became world-class through time, effort and experience. Youngsters like Anshul (Kamboj) and Gurnoor (Brar) need time and grooming to match international demands. It won’t always be 350-400 run games; bowlers will adapt to modern demands very soon,” Balaji said.Anshul Kamboj was handed his ODI debut in the third game against West Indies after Prasidh Krishna was ruled out. It was, however, a baptism of fire as he conceded 82 runs in nine overs. Gurnoor Brar, who has nine ODIs under his belt, also had an expensive series, while Auqib Nabi went for 84 in 8.5 overs on his ODI debut. Prasidh, too, had a difficult outing in his two games.Yet Balaji does not see the recent run-fests as a cause for concern.“Nothing is lacking, everyone is working hard. Since both teams have scored heavily, batting has temporarily moved ahead of bowling in modern cricket. Once bowling units click together, a balanced contest between bat and ball will return soon,” he said.
Article Summary: India 'A' coach Lakshmipathy Balaji says bowlers will adapt to modern demands. Balaji believes bowlers need time and grooming to match international demands. India begin their 2027 World Cup campaign against Australia on Oct 7 in Puducherry.

Article Title: ‘Greatest pile of mediocrity’: Matthew Hayden tears into Australia selectors over ‘disrespecting first-class cricket’
Article Text:
Matthew Hayden (Getty Images)

Hayden questions alternative options

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former Australia opener Matthew Hayden has launched a strong criticism of the national selection panel over Nic Maddinson’s recall for the three-Test series against South Africa, questioning the decision to bring back a batter who has not played first-class cricket since early 2025.Maddinson, 34, was added to Australia’s squad amid a mounting injury crisis ahead of the series opener in Durban on October 9. Josh Inglis has been ruled out with a finger injury, while Cameron Green remains a doubt for the first Test.However, Hayden believes the circumstances do not justify Maddinson’s return to the Test set-up, particularly given his lack of recent first-class cricket.Speaking on the All Over Bar The Cricket podcast, the former 103-Test opener questioned whether Maddinson would be capable of making a significant impact if Australia called upon him during the series.“Where we are at is that we are promoting the greatest pile of mediocrity that we’ve seen in a generation of cricket,” Hayden said on the All Over Bar The Cricket podcast.Hayden also took aim at chief selector George Bailey and Tony Dodemaide, arguing that Australia should be selecting players with stronger first-class records rather than relying on batters with modest averages.“And if we continue to lay that out and expect that a bloke averaging 35 is going to average 55 in Test match cricket, George Bailey and Tony Dodemaide, you are dreaming.I will just put it that simply. You are frigging dreaming. And you are piling up this dog s*** explanation, and you are, in my opinion, disrespecting first-class cricket. Absolutely dead set you are. You should be picking guys that are averaging 45 or more, and you can’t, because they don’t want to play," said Hayden.Maddinson has not featured in a Test since the 2016-17 home summer, when he scored just 27 runs across three matches. His first-class average of 37.11 has further fuelled the debate around his selection.His return to the squad comes after a difficult period that included treatment for testicular cancer.Hayden suggested Sam Harper could have been considered instead. The wicketkeeper-batter recently impressed on Australia A’s tour of India, where he also scored a century, before being added to the Test squad.The former opener also questioned the selection credentials of all-rounder Mitchell Marsh, pointing to his limited participation in state-level red-ball cricket.Hayden argued that Marsh’s lack of Shield cricket should matter despite Australia captain Pat Cummins backing the all-rounder.“I don’t care what Pat Cummins said about Mitch – if he doesn’t want to play Shield cricket … it’s a desire to front up,” Hayden said.He further criticised the growing preference among players for franchise cricket over domestic red-ball cricket, identifying it as a wider issue for Australian cricket.“They don’t want to play this version of the game. Mitch is a good example. He is making millions of dollars playing cricket all over the world for franchises. This is the fundamental problem we have," added Hayden.
Article Summary: Nic Maddinson has not played first-class cricket since early 2025. The 34-year- old has not featured in a Test since the 2016-17 home summer, when he scored just 27 runs across three matches. Hayden believes the circumstances do not justify Maddinson’s return to the Test set-up, particularly given his lack of recent first class cricket.

Article Title: ‘Game-changing approach’: ACB chief hails ILT20 management after 25 Afghan players earn contracts
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Afghanistan Cricket Board chief executive Naseeb Khan Zadran has heaped praise on the ILT20 management for its “game-changing approach” towards Afghanistan cricket after 25 Afghan players secured contracts across the league’s six franchises for Season 5.Zadran described the partnership between the ACB, Emirates Cricket Board and ILT20 as an “incredible start” and specifically credited ILT20 chairman Khalid Al Zarooni and league commissioner Mubashshir Usmani for helping create greater opportunities for Afghan cricketers.“Mr. Zarooni and Mr. Mubashshir’s vision for the growth of the game is truly inspirational, which is proven by the ILT20’s game-changing approach for both Associate Members and Full Members like Afghanistan,” Zadran said.The ACB has secured the participation of 25 Afghan players across the six franchise squads through its strategic alliance with the ECB. Under the agreement between the two boards, each franchise must include at least four Afghan players in its squad, while the Season 5 playing conditions require a minimum of two Afghan players in every playing XI.The provisions have created defined opportunities for Afghan cricketers at both squad and match level, with established internationals and emerging players set to feature in the UAE-based competition.The auction attracted strong interest in Afghan players, with Fazalhaq Farooqi and Rahmanullah Gurbaz among the leading signings. Zadran said the two had earned “record amounts of money” through the bidding.“The auction has raised the profile of Afghanistan cricket and players like never before. A total of 25 Afghanistan players have earned contracts with the DP World ILT20 franchises, with Fazalhaq Farooqi and Rahmanullah Gurbaz earning record amounts of money through their massive bidding amounts,” he said.Zadran also credited the partnership with the ILT20 and ECB for providing a professional pathway for Afghan players and helping expand the game in the country.“This opportunity for our players is a result of our incredible partnership with the DP World ILT20 and the Emirates Cricket Board,” he said. “We reached a strategic decision with them earlier this year with an aim of further expanding the game in Afghanistan through the ILT20/ECB’s support.”He also singled out Al Zarooni and Usmani for their role in implementing the partnership.“I want to take this opportunity to thank the Chairman ILT20 Khalid Al Zarooni and League Commissioner Mubashshir Usmani, who were instrumental in the implementation and execution of this partnership,” Zadran said.Zadran added that the ACB was confident the partnership would continue to benefit Afghan cricket.“We are off to an incredible start in our partnership, and we have full confidence that this partnership will continue to support our players and inspire a new generation of Afghanistan stars,” he said.
Article Summary: Afghanistan Cricket Board chief executive Naseeb Khan Zadran heaps praise on the ILT20 management. 25 Afghan players secured contracts across the league’s six franchises for Season 5. Fazalhaq Farooqi and Rahmanullah Gurbaz among the leading signings.

SA20 auction 2026 : Time and where to watch

The SA20 Season 5 Player Auction will take place on Wednesday, with four franchises set to fill 19 remaining slots and a combined $2.10 million available to spend.Durban’s Super Giants and Paarl Royals have already completed their squad-building after the league increased the salary cap to $2.54 million for the upcoming season.Among the four teams heading into the auction, Joburg Super Kings have the biggest purse with $1.245 million available. MI Cape Town have $565,150, Sunrisers Eastern Cape have $217,600, while Pretoria Capitals have just $89,150 remaining.Joburg Super Kings and MI Cape Town must each sign one Under-23 player from the final shortlist of 48 players. Joburg also have a wildcard slot still available.There will be no Right to Match cards at the Season 5 auction.Each team must have 19 players in its registered squad, comprising 18 regular squad members and one wildcard player.The 18-player squad can have a maximum of seven overseas players and must include at least 11 South African players, with two of those required to be Under-23 players.The wildcard can be either a South African or overseas player and will not count towards the salary cap.The auction will feature marquee mixed-set rounds followed by a nomination express round, in which teams can call up the player they want to bid for.The auction takes place on October 7, with SA20 Season 5 following a previous edition in which Dewald Brevis became the league's most expensive player after Pretoria Capitals bought him for R16.5 million.Matthew Breetzke is another player whose auction value has risen significantly. Durban’s Super Giants initially signed him for his base price of $10,576 at the inaugural auction before Sunrisers Eastern Cape bought him for $368,000 three seasons later.The Season 5 Player Auction begins at 8:30pm IST on Wednesday, October 7.In India, the auction will be broadcast on JioHotstar. It will also be streamed live on the official SA20 YouTube channel.

Article Title: ‘We’re not trying to be any other league’: SA20 COO Lynn Naudé on the league’s rapid rise
Article Text:
Lynn Naudé (left), COO of SA20 (Special Arrangement)

Excerpts

SA20 has grown rapidly in four seasons. What has been the biggest lesson behind that success?

How do you keep SA20 distinct in an increasingly crowded global T20 calendar?

What role has the league played in strengthening South African cricket beyond the professional level?

With overseas leagues expanding, how do you ensure SA20 continues attracting elite international players?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Looking ahead to Season 5, what is the one area where you want fans to notice a clear step forward?

NEW DELHI: Four seasons into its existence, SA20 has already established itself as one of the most prominent T20 leagues outside the IPL. But for COO Lynn Naudé, the league’s rapid rise has been less about chasing quick wins and more about getting the fundamentals right. From securing a prime South African summer window and putting Proteas at the heart of the competition to creating a strong match-day atmosphere, Naudé explains how SA20 has built its identity and what lies ahead in Season 5.I think probably the biggest lesson is that strong foundations matter more than quick wins. From the very start, we were very single-minded about what we believed success looked like. The fan experience, the quality of cricket and putting South African players at the heart of the competition were all important to us. We wanted to make sure SA20 felt like it belonged to South African fans as a starting point, and then we could take it global from there.I think that's probably been one of my biggest learnings. If you can get your basics right, the rest will follow from thereT20 cricket has got a unique feeling to it, and that's possibly a common thread. But I think there are a couple of things that have helped us.First, our window and our ability to secure it in the heart of the South African summer, with great conditions and full stadiums, was a real coup for us.That time of year lends itself to delivering a product that speaks very much to the fans, but also provides a fantastic experience both on broadcast and in the stadium.The second is the quality of the competition. The commitment from Cricket South Africa to make all of its Proteas available to play in the tournament season after season, and to see them compete with the best in the world, means that we have intentionally put cricket at the heart of the product.The third is probably the atmosphere at the venues. I think that's become something quite synonymous with SA20.If I had to wrap it up, I'd say we're not trying to be any other league. We're just trying to be the best version of SA20 that we can be.”It has actually been on multiple levels. The intention was for SA20 to almost become a bastion for South African cricket. There was obviously work that needed to be done to strengthen the talent pipeline.But outside of that, if I look back again on the last five seasons, it's also about the quality of the broadcast, what's improved in terms of the fan experience within the South African sporting context, our venues, the ways of working and how they operate on a day-to-day basis.There's also been a lot of knowledge transfer from SA20 into the greater cricket ecosystem, with some of the standards and expectations that we have for the type of product we want to deliver.We've had the opportunity to expose a lot of young talent in the sporting industry to our ways of working and the culture at SA20.In the lead-up to the 2027 World Cup, what we've tried to do is make sure that the cricket ecosystem, and those who deliver not only on the field but also off it, is better off the back of SA20 and the experience it has brought to the South African cricket landscape.At the highest level, elite players want to play where the cricket is competitive, the conditions are good and the environment is professional. I think that's something we strive to offer, and I think we do offer all three.Our franchises bring global experience and know how to run teams. The players know that when they come here, they'll be tested against strong domestic talent and they'll be playing in front of full stadiums.It's always surprising to me, anecdotally, when I hear players talk about how important it is to them to play in front of a crowd and how different it feels. I guess when you're talented like that, you feel appreciated when you're playing in front of a lot of people.That, coupled with the strong and stable franchise ownership groups that we've got, who invest in those players, offers them opportunities.If you have the opportunity to play in the SA20, you also have the opportunity to play in many other places around the world. I think consistency across all of those things will make sure that we remain attractive to players.Every season we run a fan survey, and it directly shapes what we deliver. Our fans have told us what they want to see more of, and they've also told us what they don't want us to change. Those are the types of things that shape our decisions.Our brand positioning at SA20 is ‘for everyone’, and we take that pretty seriously. On the field, it means competitive, world-class cricket for the dedicated cricket fan. Off the field, it really means a great social occasion for people to come and enjoy the atmosphere, the music and a day out with friends and family.If I have to say what I want fans to take away, it's that we do hear you, we do listen to what you want, and we will always strive to deliver based on the feedback that fans are giving us.
Article Summary: Lynn Naudé, COO of SA20, talks to TOI about the league's rapid rise. SA20 has established itself as one of the most prominent T20 leagues outside the IPL. COO says league's success has been down to getting the fundamentals right. He talks about securing a prime South African summer window.

Article Title: 'Real-life hero': Sachin Tendulkar, Yuvraj Singh lead cricket fraternity in hailing Captain Smit Machchhar after saving 174 lives
Article Text:
Smit Machchhar

'A true real-life hero': Sachin Tendulkar

Raina hails 'son of Gujarat'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Sehwag praises his courage under pressure

Yuvraj: 'Some moments show you what a person is truly made of'

NEW DELHI: The courage of Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar, who was seriously injured while trying to prevent a potential catastrophe aboard flydubai Flight FZ1073, has earned admiration from across the country, including some of India's biggest cricketing names.Sachin Tendulkar, Yuvraj Singh, Suresh Raina and Virender Sehwag were among the former India cricketers who took to social media to salute Machchhar for his bravery and presence of mind during the terrifying mid-air incident.Machchhar was the captain of the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight when a violent confrontation reportedly broke out in the cockpit on Wednesday. According to reports, he was attacked by his co-pilot but, despite suffering serious injuries, managed to help open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew members to intervene. The aircraft was subsequently diverted and landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. All 174 people aboard were reported safe.Tendulkar was among the first prominent cricketers to acknowledge Machchhar's courage."Learnt about the incredible bravery of Captain Smit Machchhar. Immense courage in the face of a terrifying and unprecedented challenge. A true real-life hero. The entire world is proud of you," Tendulkar wrote.Former India batter Suresh Raina also paid tribute to Machchhar, highlighting the captain's courage despite being seriously injured."A true hero, a proud moment for India! Salute to Captain Smit Machchhar, a son of Gujarat, whose extraordinary courage and presence of mind, even while seriously injured, helped save 174 precious lives," Raina wrote.Virender Sehwag highlighted the extraordinary circumstances in which Machchhar continued to act despite his injuries."In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others," Sehwag wrote.Yuvraj Singh also joined the tributes, focusing on Machchhar's decision to put the safety of others ahead of his own."Some moments show you what a person is truly made of," Yuvraj wrote.Machchhar, who has more than 13 years of commercial flying experience and previously worked with SpiceJet before joining flydubai in 2022, is currently recovering after undergoing treatment in Saudi Arabia.
Article Summary: Captain Smit Machchhar was seriously injured while trying to prevent a potential catastrophe aboard flydubai Flight FZ1073. Sachin Tendulkar, Yuvraj Singh, Suresh Raina and Virender Sehwag took to social media to pay tribute to the pilot's bravery. All 174 people aboard the flight were reported safe.

The SA20 Season 5 auction will see 156 cricketers go under the hammer on October 7, with former Joburg Super Kings captain Faf du Plessis Rassie van der Dussen and all-rounder Wiaan Mulder among the leading South African names available.The shortlist was trimmed down from 789 players who initially registered for the auction. Of the 156 players remaining, 95 are South African and 61 are overseas cricketers, with 19 squad places still available across four of the six franchises.Durban's Super Giants and Paarl Royals have already completed their 19-player squads and will not participate in the auction. Joburg Super Kings and MI Cape Town have six slots each to fill, while Pretoria Capitals have five and Sunrisers Eastern Cape have two.JSK and MI Cape Town also have the largest purses available, with $1.24 million and $562,813, respectively. Sunrisers Eastern Cape have $216,699 remaining, while Pretoria Capitals have $88,786.Among the leading South African players in the pool are du Plessis, Mulder, fast bowler Nandre Burger and veteran batter van der Dussen. Du Plessis, who previously led JSK, continues to feature prominently in franchise cricket and recently finished as the leading run-scorer in Europe.The two Under-23 slots are also expected to attract significant interest. Fast bowler Matthew Boast, who commanded the joint-highest bid at the Season 2 auction, is among the players in this category, alongside former South Africa Under-19 captain Jason Rowles.The first four SA20 auctions have produced several significant deals. Tristan Stubbs fetched $554,693 at the inaugural auction, while Dewald Brevis set a new record with a $994,834 deal last season.The auction has also provided a route for several South African players to gain exposure to international franchise cricket, with some subsequently securing further opportunities on the global T20 circuit.The overseas contingent includes former West Indies captain Kieron Pollard, New Zealand pacer Trent Boult, Shimron Hetmyer, Shamar Joseph, Mohammad Nabi, AM Ghazanfar, Jordan Cox, Aneurin Donald, Rehan Ahmed and Richard Gleeson.Several established T20 names are already part of the six franchises, including Jos Buttler, Joe Root, Sam Curran, Sunil Narine, Kane Williamson, Andre Russell, Sherfane Rutherford, Mitchell Marsh and Phil Salt.The auction will be broadcast live on SuperSport at 5pm SAST, JioStar at 8.30pm IST, Sky Sports at 4pm BST, Apex at 7.30pm PKT, Fox Sports at 11pm AEDT and Willow TV at 11am ET. The event will also be streamed live on the SA20 YouTube channel.

Former Joburg Super Kings captain Faf du Plessis and all-rounder Wiaan Mulder are among the leading South African names available. Of the 156 players remaining, 95 are South African and 61 are overseas.

Ash Gardner has spoken publicly for the first time about the alleged affair with teammate Georgia Voll that contributed to the breakdown of her marriage to Monica Wright.Gardner said the situation became far more public than she expected and admitted she had been “naive” about the level of attention it would attract.The controversy came to light earlier this year when Wright revealed the affair on social media. A change of guard formally took place in Indian women’s cricket on Tuesday as Harmanpreet Kaur , 37, stepped down as captain across all three formats and was replaced by Smriti Mandhana , 30.Harmanpreet, who captained India to its first women’s global title in the 2025 ODI World Cup and most recently led the team’s successful defence of the Asian Games gold medal, announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post. She said she would continue as a player and was “ready to play for the love of the game again”.Harmanpreet was reportedly offered the option of continuing as ODI captain but chose to give up leadership across formats. Her decision was not entirely unexpected, with pressure building over India’s T20I results and her own recent form.The Indian cricket board ( BCCI ) announced Mandhana as India’s new captain across formats on Tuesday evening.The announcement came a day after Harmanpreet, Mandhana, head coach Amol Muzumdar and the national selectors met BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia in Guwahati to review the women’s team’s performance since June and discuss the roadmap ahead of the inaugural Women’s Champions Trophy in India next February. They met again on Tuesday.“Today, I step down as captain of the Indian women’s cricket team across all formats.This is not an easy decision,” Harmanpreet wrote, adding, “It carries years of memories, emotions, sacrifices and moments that will stay with me for the rest of my life. I’ve given everything I had to this team and to Indian women’s cricket — my blood, my sweat, my time, and many times, a part of my own game and personal ambitions.”Harmanpreet said every decision she made as captain was driven by the team’s interests.“I leave the captaincy today with a heart full of emotions, but also with peace,” she wrote. “Because I genuinely believe my team is in a good place — a team with talent, character, belief and a future that I am incredibly excited to watch and be a part of.”New captain Mandhana, who was vice-captain under Harmanpreet, has been in prolific form in recent years and is the leading run-getter in women’s cricket across formats, with 11,066 runs in 308 matches. She also leads the run charts in women’s T20Is with 4,867 runs in 172 games.Mandhana has also captained Royal Challengers Bengaluru to two Women’s Premier League titles, in 2024 and 2026. In an interview with TOI on July 15, she had said she was “ready for the India captaincy”.“I’d like to acknowledge Harmanpreet and the contribution she has made as captain over the years. She has led the team with great commitment and has been an important part of our journey. I understand the responsibility that comes with the role,” Mandhana was quoted as saying in a BCCI statement.Harmanpreet’s captaincy came under scrutiny after India’s league-stage exit at the 2026 Women’s T20 World Cup in June, following a similar disappointment in the UAE in 2024. Her returns with the bat had also dipped — 71 runs in five matches at the 2026 Asia Cup and 59 runs in three matches at the Asian Games.India, however, responded strongly under her, winning the one-off Test against England at Lord’s in July, the Asia Cup in the UAE and defending their Asian Games gold in Japan last month. That triumph in Nisshin was Harmanpreet’s final act as captain.Harmanpreet captained India for a decade — in five Tests, 51 ODIs and 155 T20Is. She first led India in T20Is in 2012, became full-time T20I captain in 2016 and was in charge when India reached the semi-finals of the 2018 Women’s T20 World Cup and the final in 2020. She took over the ODI captaincy in 2022 after Mithali Raj moved on and became India’s all-format skipper in 2023.In ODIs, Harmanpreet won 30 of her 51 matches as captain. Her crowning moment came at the 2025 Women’s World Cup, where India mounted a dramatic turnaround and beat South Africa in the final in Navi Mumbai. Harmanpreet also took the catch that sealed the title.During her tenure, India won three Asia Cups, the 2025 ODI World Cup, two Asian Games gold medals and a Commonwealth Games silver.Former India captain Diana Edulji called Harmanpreet’s decision “a step in the right direction”.“It’s time to move on. Harman has performed well as captain. She has taken the Indian women’s cricket team to the highest level,” Edulji told TOI.
Article Summary: Harmanpreet Kaur steps down as captain of India women's cricket team. Smriti Mandhana is replaced as captain across all three formats. Harman preet captained India to its first women’s global title in 2025 ODI World Cup.

India’s 21-gold campaign at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games has thrown up an interesting set of numbers: champions who reached the continental podium despite receiving relatively modest targeted financial assistance under the govt’s elite-athlete programmes.Their stories do not diminish the broader support extended to Indian sport. Instead, they underline how performances can sometimes run ahead of the funding pipelines designed to identify and back medal prospects.The clearest example is 17-year-old archer Kumkum Mohod. A recently-inducted Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS) athlete for the Aich-Nagoya preparatory cycle, Kumkum became the first Indian woman to win an individual recurve gold at the Games, defeating South Korea’s Oh Yejin 6-5 after a shoot-off. She also won gold in the women’s recurve team event and silver in mixed team, ending the campaign with three medals and securing India an LA Olympics quota.The funding support extended to her puts her targeted assistance at just Rs 50,000. That is a striking figure against the scale of her achievement, even though her preparation also benefited from the budget allocated to the respective national sports federations (NSFs) under the Annual Calendar for Training and Competition (ACTC).The same pattern is visible in compound archery. Sahil Rajesh Jadhav, who helped India win mixed team gold with Chikitha Taniparthi and also contributed to the men’s team gold, received Rs 50,000 under TOPS during the Games cycle. His top podium finish also delivered India an Olympic quota in compound archery.Kushal Dalal and Thirumuru Ganesh Maniratnam, members of India’s men’s compound team that defeated China for gold, also received only Rs 50,000 each under TOPS during the cycle. Yet the trio of Dalal, Ganesh and Jadhav produced one of India’s five archery gold medals at the Games.The contrast becomes sharper when placed alongside athletes receiving substantially larger targeted allocations. Boxer Ankush Panghal, for instance, received Rs 75,000 under TOPS, while his other gold partners in boxing Lovlina Borgohain and Parveen Hooda received Rs 22.97 lakh and Rs 8.59 lakh assistance, respectively, during the Games cycle.These figures show that support was available at markedly different levels depending on an athlete’s classification, requirements, and timing within the system.Similarly, in sailing, Harshita Tomar and Shital Verma secured the bronze medal in the women’s skiff, with both athletes not being part of the TOPS programme. Also, in the same sport, sailors Manu Francis and Prince Noble won silver in the men’s skiff, but both were not part of either TOPS Core or Development group. Boxer Kapil Pokhariya, too, wasn't part of the TOPS.In shooting, the trio of Manisha Keer, Neeru Dhanda and Aashima Ahlawat won the silver medal in Trap women's team event, with Manisha receiving no TOPS assistance while Neeru, a TOPS Development athlete, getting Rs one lakh. In athletics, silver-wining javelin thrower Yashvir Singh wasn't part of the TOPS funding and largely prepared through the ACTC budget. In kurash, bronze-winner Pincky Balhara, competing in the -78 kg event, received Rs 75,000 under the TAGG scheme during the Games cycle.Kumkum Mohod (Rs 50,000), Sahil Jadhav (Rs 50,000), Kushal Dalal (Rs 50,000), Thirumuru Maniratnam (Rs 50,000),Ankush (Rs 75,000), Kapil Pokhariya (not covered under TOPS);Neeru Dhanda (Rs 1,00,000),Pincky Balhara (Rs 75,000),Seema (Rs 25,000), Baranica Elangoan and Yashvir Singh (both not covered under TOPS).

The funding support extended to her puts her targeted assistance at just Rs 50,000. The contrast becomes sharper when placed alongside athletes receiving substantially larger targeted allocations.

NEW DELHI: Lovlina Borgohain ’s Asian Games gold was not just a medal upgrade from silver in the last edition. It was the latest marker in a 15-year career that has taken the Assam boxer through Olympic success, injuries, difficult phases and a mentally demanding Paris 2024 campaign.At the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Borgohain finally changed the colour of her Asian Games medal, defeating China’s Bao Ziyi 5-0 in the women’s 75kg final. The victory, on her 29th birthday, made her only the second Indian woman after MC Mary Kom to win boxing gold at the Asian Games -- 12 years after Kom’s 2014 triumph.For Borgohain, however, the gold's significance went beyond the history books.“It’s still difficult to get out of this moment. I still have the gold medal in my hand," said a beaming Borgohain while lifting the gold medal next to her face. "It’s a very special moment for me. I can’t express how I feel,” she continued as she spoke to TimesofIndia.com upon returning from Japan.Borgohain had finished with silver at the 2022 Hangzhou Asian Games, losing to China’s Li Qian in the final. Three years later, she returned to the continental stage determined to go one step further.Her path to the gold in Nagoya was not straightforward. She began with a 5-0 quarter-final win over South Korea’s Seong Su-yeon before edging Kazakhstan’s reigning 70kg world champion Natalya Bogdanova 3-2 in a closely fought semi-final.She then produced a 5-0 win over Ziyi in the final.The contrast with Hangzhou made the medal particularly meaningful.“Every event is very important. We believe that the Asian Games medal is the highest after the Olympics. I think this medal is shining amidst all the medals. The colour has changed. This medal means a lot to me,” Borgohain said.“I got a silver medal in the last Asian Games and this time I got a gold medal. This is why it is so special. And to do it on my birthday is extra special.”The victory also continued a curious connection between Borgohain and Japan. Five years ago, Tokyo had brought her an Olympic bronze medal — the breakthrough that changed the trajectory of her career.“I was very excited because I was going to Japan again. I had won a medal in (the) 2020 Olympics in Japan, and my life changed because of that,” she said.“I had a positive mindset before leaving India. I wanted to make it the best tournament of my life. I knew that I could do it because Japan is lucky for me.”The gold also offered a reminder of Borgohain’s ability to rebuild.Her career has not followed a straight line since the Tokyo Olympics. Injuries, changes in form and the disappointment of the Paris Olympics tested her, while the pressure that came with becoming an Olympic medallist added another layer to the challenge.Borgohain does not, however, see the Asian Games gold as something that has fundamentally changed her.“I don’t think I am looking at myself differently because of this medal. I have won and lost a lot of medals. People’s perspective changes because of the medal. But I am always the same in my own eyes,” she said.“My perspective has not changed because of the medal. When I lose, my self-belief remains the same. Sometimes I am confident, and sometimes I am down. But I am the same person that I was before.”That mindset became particularly important after Paris 2024, when she failed to reach the medal rounds. Borgohain describes the period as one of the most difficult phases of her career.“I have a 15-year journey. Every time I go to a competition, my mindset is different. When we play, we reach the medal. It is not easy to recover from a tough period. The 2024 Paris Olympics wasn’t an easy period for me mentally,” she said.“But I think everything is a game of the mind. It depends on how we look at it. If we take tough things easy, it becomes easy. If we take easy things hard, it becomes hard. I think that helped me a lot to keep myself calm and relaxed.”The Asian Games victory has also given Borgohain a more direct route towards the next stage of her career. The gold means she qualifies for the World Championships, rather than having to go through the national selection route. A strong performance there could also put her on the road to another Olympic qualification campaign.“It matters a lot for an athlete because of this medal I am qualifying for the World Championships. I am getting a good treat otherwise I would have to play the Nationals and follow the same process,” she said.“So that is a big advantage of the medal, and it boosts my confidence that I can do better. If I do well there, then I can qualify for the Olympics also.”For now, though, Borgohain is resisting the temptation to look too far ahead.“There is a lot of planning. But not everything is the same. I am living in the present. I don’t know what will happen tomorrow. I will try to live like this. It makes me feel good. I will try to live like this.”Borgohain’s gold was part of a strong boxing campaign for India at the Asian Games. India finished the competition with six boxing medals, including three golds, with Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal also winning their respective finals.Some months back, Indian boxers had returned with 10 medals at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, including seven golds. No country had won more golds in boxing at a single edition of the CWG. It was also India's largest haul in the sport in a CWG.For Borgohain, the improvement reflects a broader change in the mentality of Indian boxers.“We had a very good performance. Both men and women did very well. Everyone knows the results of the Commonwealth Games. The results of the Commonwealth Games changed the results of Indian Boxing,” she said.“In the Asian Games, our Indian team came out on top. I think our athletes are very strong. Their mentality is very good. We used to think that we would not be able to do it. But now our young athletes have the mindset that ‘we have to do it’.”She also pointed to the support structure around the team, including government backing and the environment created by the coaching staff led by Santiago Nieva.“The support of the government matters a lot. They don’t let us down. We are getting good competition. The environment of our foreign coaches, led by Santiago (Nieva), is very positive. That is why we are getting good results.”For Borgohain, then, the Asian Games gold is both an ending and a beginning — the end of a 12-year wait since Mary Kom’s historic gold and the completion of a personal journey from Hangzhou silver to Nagoya gold.But she is not treating it as a destination. The next target can wait. For now, she is content to live in the moment — with the gold medal still in her hand.
Article Summary: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain won gold at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya. She beat China's Bao Ziyi 5-0 in the women's 75kg final. The victory, on her 29th birthday, made her only the second Indian woman after Mary Kom to win boxing gold.

Article Title: Vithya Ramraj on newfound fame: 'I'm still far away from reaching world standards'
Article Text:

CHENNAI: With three medals and newfound recognition, Vithya Ramraj returned home from the Asian Games with plenty to celebrate. People at petrol bunks, airports and bus stands have started recognizing her, but it has left the 28-year old, who broke P T Usha’s 400 metre 42-year-old hurdles record, slightly surprised.“People are recognising me now and I’m happy athletics is growing. I’m also thinking about the recognition I am getting. Is it because of the relay medals or because I broke the record? Why have I become famous? That is one constant thing on my mind. I’m still far away from reaching world standards, and my coach was not happy with the timing.“Personally, I didn’t get the satisfaction even though people celebrated. I think of how Neeraj Chopra is celebrated, and if I reach his level, then more people will know me,” Vithya told TOI.What worked for Vithya in 400m hurdles was that she brought down her stride count from 17 to 16 between hurdles 5 and 6.“In the bend from the fifth to the sixth hurdle, I used to take 17 strides, but I have now reduced it to 16. We have been working on it since Nov last year. That helped me going into the home stretch.”Going into the Asian Games, Vithya did not dip below 56 seconds even once this season. While she bagged gold at the Federation Cup and Inter-state athletics meet, her coach Nehpal Singh, who has been a strong source of support, was not satisfied with the medals.“My coach told me, ‘Did I train you to run 56 seconds? What performance have you put in?’”What Vithya felt helped her in the run-up to the Asian Games was the training stints she had in Poland and the Czech Republic with Nehpal.“I used to sleep for 10 hours for three months during the stint abroad, but in India, I used to sleep only for 7-8 hours. In India, I cannot train at 10 am due to the climate, but the sleep cycle in Poland helped me. In India, I train from 5:30am to 8:30am,” she said.
Article Summary: Vithya Ramraj won three medals at the Asian Games. She broke P T Usha’s 400 metre 42-year-old hurdles record. Her coach Nehpal Singh was not satisfied with the medals. Vithya felt training in Poland and the Czech Republic helped her.

NEW DELHI: Two years ago, Sujeet Kalkal was stranded at Dubai International Airport, watching his Olympic dream slip away with every passing hour.On his way to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, for the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament, Kalkal was stuck in Dubai for three days after floods disrupted his travel plans. By the time a flight was arranged, it was too late. He could not reach Bishkek in time, and with it went his chance to qualify for the Paris Olympics.Two years later, the disappointment of Dubai has been replaced by an Asian Games gold. Kalkal, the world No. 2 in the men's 65kg category, fought back from 2-9 down against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev in the final to win 10-9, ending India's eight-year wait for a wrestling gold at the Games.The comeback was symbolic of what Kalkal's career has looked like since that Olympic setback. He has had to rebuild, compete through the disappointment and find a way back to the biggest stages. On Sunday, he did that with an Asian Games title.When the final whistle came, Kalkal folded his hands, looked up and thanked God. He then took a lap of the arena with the Indian tricolour draped around his shoulders, tears and a broad smile.For a wrestler who had once been denied even the chance to fight for an Olympic place, the moment carried a little more weight than an Asian Games gold."This gold means a lot to me. Not just because it is an Asian Games gold, but because there is so much behind this medal. The last few years have had many ups and downs, and I missed a few opportunities, but I never lost belief in myself," Kalkal told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview on his way back to Imlota village in Bhiwani, Haryana, where his parents were waiting to welcome him.The Dubai episode, he says, is now behind him. What remains is the lesson from it - and a much bigger target."Paris was very difficult for me to miss, but that experience made me stronger instead of breaking me. LA 2028 is obviously a very big goal for me," Kalkal said.And he is clear about what he wants from that opportunity. "Olympics mein jaana hai toh sirf participate karne ke liye nahi jaana, bhaisaab. Gold ke liye jaana hai [“If you’re going to the Olympics, don’t go just to participate, brother. Go there to win gold]."India had not won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games since 2018. Kalkal's victory ended that wait and added another major title to a career that already includes an U23 World Championship crown, Asian Championships success and a Zagreb Open triumph."India has won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games after eight years, so being a part of it is very special for me. This medal reminds me that if you keep working hard, your time will come," he said.The road to the Asian Games gold was not easy for Kalkal. He had a challenging draw, but handled each bout with confidence.After a comfortable opening victory, he made a statement in the quarterfinals by throwing Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi from a standing position within the opening 20 seconds.The semifinal brought an even bigger test, but Kalkal overcame Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka to reach the gold medal bout.Then came the final against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev, and it looked like the toughest challenge of them all.Instead of allowing the deficit to affect him, Kalkal fought his way back into the contest. He produced eight points to turn a seven-point deficit into a 10-9 victory and seal the Asian Games title."The simple plan was to wrestle my own way and not be impressed by my opponent's name. Whether he is an Olympic champion, a world champion or anyone else, everyone starts from zero on the mat. I just trusted my preparation and my strength. I knew that if I executed my best, I could beat anyone. Instead of thinking too much during the match, I just had to fight for every single point," he said.Kalkal also dedicated the gold to the country and remembered his father, who stood by him throughout his journey."I dedicate this gold to the whole of India. Of course, my first call was to my father. He has supported me tremendously throughout this journey, and without his support, it would have been impossible for me to reach this point. His support will always remain with me," the Indian wrestler said.The final also reflected the mental change Kalkal says came from the disappointment of 2024."Fear may never completely go away, but now I know how to fight with fear. When you go through tough situations in life, small things stop bothering you. What happened in Dubai, missing the Olympic qualifiers - every experience taught me something," the Indian wrestler said."Now I don't run away from pressure. I enjoy pressure because those are the moments when you realise how strong you actually are," Kalkal said.The Asian Games gold now joins an already impressive list of achievements for Kalkal, but he is not dwelling on the medals he has already won. The next target is Los Angeles. And this time, he wants to get there on his own terms."Gold ke liye jaana hai."
Article Summary: Two years ago, Sujeet Kalkal was stranded at Dubai International Airport. He was on his way to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, for the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament. Two years later, the disappointment of Dubai has been replaced by an Asian Games gold. He fought back from 2-9 down against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev.

Article Title: Other side of India's Asian Games success: 201 athletes won just 6 bronze, 137 returned empty-handed
Article Text:
AP Photo

The spending breakdown

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India’s 85-medal haul at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games was its secondbest finish, but the headline numbers don’t reveal everything.A sport-by-sport audit by TOI shows that 137 Indian athletes across 16 disciplines returned empty-handed, exposing persistent gaps in the country’s medal ambitions.India’s pruned-down 495-member contingent competed across 36 sport disciplines and finished fourth with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals.Yet 137 athletes across 16 disciplines won nothing.Another 64 athletes across six sports managed six bronze — one each in kurash, mixed martial arts, rowing, sepaktakraw, soft tennis and wushu. The zero-medal list included canoeing (19 athletes), cycling (14), equestrian (7), esports (15), fencing (20), gymnastics (1), judo (3), karate (2), rugby sevens (13), sport climbing (2), surfing (4), swimming (12), taekwondo (3), tennis (7), teqball (3) and volleyball (12). The six-bronze group comprised kurash (6 athletes), MMA (2), rowing (22), sepaktakraw (21), soft tennis (6) and wushu (7).In all, 201 athletes accounted for just six bronze medals across the 22 disciplines mentioned above. In other prominent sports with sizable athlete numbers, table tennis sent 10 athletes and returned with one bronze and badminton’s 20-member contingent managed one bronze in the men’s team event.Together, the two sent 37 athletes and produced only two bronze.India contested in 259 medal events in AichiNagoya and won medals in just 20, a 7.7% eventpodium conversion rate. Of 356 medals available in which India featured, the nation collected 85, a conversion rate of only 23.9%.The govt spent Rs 259.69 crore on 19 sports as part of the overall total expenditure during the current Asian Games cycle (Nov 2023-Aug 2026), led by badminton (Rs 49.26 cr), cycling track (Rs 35.9 cr), fencing (Rs 28.2 cr), table tennis (Rs 25.3 cr), tennis (Rs 22.4 cr) and canoe/kayak (Rs 20.1 cr). Other allocations included rowing (Rs 13.8 cr,) swimming (Rs 10.8 cr), gymnastics (Rs 10.49 cr), judo (Rs 8.05 cr), wushu (Rs 7.8 cr), volleyball (Rs 6.5 cr), sepaktakraw (Rs 5.7 cr), equestrian (Rs 3.7 cr), rugby (Rs 3.63 cr), surfing (Rs 2.9 cr), karate (Rs 1.99 cr), soft tennis (Rs 1.6 cr) and kurash (Rs 1.6 cr).On three sports – MMA, eSports and sport climbing, the govt spent no money. As per the govt’s own estimates, it spent approximately Rs 703 cr across 30 disciplines during the Nov 2023-Aug 2026 preparation cycle. The Rs 703 cr included about Rs 118 cr for domestic training and national coaching camps, Rs 40 cr for overseas training, Rs 252 cr for international competition exposure, Rs 89 cr for equipment, Rs 86 cr for foreign coaches/support staff and Rs 118 cr for other expenses, including Indian experts, championships, competitions in India, grassroots and coach development.Also, a total of 427 athletes who were part of the govt’s various programmes and schemes participated in the Games, including 77 athletes from Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS) Core group, 78 from TOPS Development 78, 48 from Target Asian Games Group (TAGG), 65 Khelo India Athlete (KIA), 25 from National Centre of Excellence (NCoE) and 134 from National Coaching Camps (NCCs).The Glasgow comparison is revealing, though not like-for-like. India had 122 athletes and para-athletes in 10 sports at the curtailed 2026 Commonwealth Games and won 39 medals — 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze — also finishing fourth. The Asian Games contingent was 4.06 times larger, but its 85-medal haul was only 2.18 times Glasgow’s. Medal efficiency was 17.2 per 100 athletes in Aichi-Nagoya against 32 in Glasgow.The message is that at this level, the medal base remains concentrated.For a country investing Rs 703 cr across a multi-year cycle, the next challenge is clear: turn wider participation, exposure and support into wider podium conversion.
Article Summary: India’s pruned-down 495-member contingent competed across 36 sport disciplines and finished fourth with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. Of 356 medals available in which India featured, the nation collected 85, a conversion rate of only 23.9%. The govt spent Rs 259.69 crore on 19 sports as part of the overall total expenditure during the current Asian Games cycle.

Article Title: World champion beaten, Olympic champion toppled at Asian Games: Wrestlers dream of hearing India’s national anthem at the LA Olympics
Article Text:
India's gold-medallist wrestlers - Sujeet Kalkal and Aman Sehrawat.

Sehrawat turns a difficult phase into gold

Aman Sehrawat

Kalkal follows gold with an Olympic-sized ambition

India's Sujeet Kalkal, right, competes in the final against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev in the Asian Games. (PTI Photo)

From selling milk to a historic Greco-Roman final

Nitesh Siwach (Image credit: X)

Punia battles through a new weight category

Deepak Punia (ANI Photo)

Panghal improves on Hangzhou, Kumar makes history

Antim Panghal

Six medals, one bigger dream

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India's wrestlers arrived in Aichi-Nagoya carrying questions over injuries, form and confidence. They left with six medals — two gold, two silver and two bronze — and a much bigger target already occupying their minds: the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Aman Sehrawat and Sujeet Kalkal struck gold, while Nitesh Siwach and Antim Panghal won silver and Deepak Punia and Sunil Kumar added bronze.The campaign was also marked by two major statements. Sehrawat defeated reigning world champion Han Chong Song in the men's 57kg freestyle final, while Kalkal beat Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka on his way to gold in the 65kg category.For the Indian wrestlers, however, Nagoya was less about looking back at what they had achieved and more about building towards what comes next.For Sehrawat, the gold was the culmination of one of the most difficult phases of his young career.The 23-year-old had won bronze at the Paris Olympics but subsequently struggled with motivation in 2025. A persistent stomach ailment also forced him to miss important competitions.In Nagoya, however, Sehrawat rediscovered his best. He defeated reigning world champion Han Chong Song 11-7 in the final, recovering after the North Korean had turned a 1-6 deficit into a 7-6 lead.It was Sehrawat's first Asian Games gold after his bronze at Hangzhou."Ups and downs, injuries keep happening like this. That phase also comes, but I had the belief in my mind. We should never give up, and I did the same. Today, I have won a gold medal in the Games. The future goal is the Olympics," Sehrawat said after returning to India.He said the next goal was to replicate the achievement on the biggest stage."We won gold for the country. The plan for the future is exactly the same — we will win gold for the country and prepare accordingly. I thank all the countrymen; it was their prayers that worked in the matches," he added.Then came the statement that perhaps best captured the mood of India's wrestling contingent."...now we will do better in the future. The whole nation is giving us love. Now our national anthem will be played at the LA Olympics."If Sehrawat's gold was a comeback story, Kalkal's was a lesson in refusing to surrender.The world No. 2 entered the Asian Games unbeaten this season and lived up to his billing in the men's 65kg freestyle category.Before the final, Kalkal defeated Japan's Olympic champion Kiyooka and Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi. Against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev in the final, he appeared to be heading towards defeat after falling 2-9 behind.Instead, he produced a stunning late comeback to win 10-9.The victory restored India's hold on the 65kg Asian Games title, a category in which Yogeshwar Dutt and Bajrang Punia had previously won gold."Whatever struggle I did has paid off. The final match was tough, but I was only thinking of winning that time," Kalkal said.His sights are already firmly fixed on Los Angeles."Now we will practice more, and if all goes well, we will win gold at the Olympics too. For the Olympics, the practice has already begun," Kalkal added.Nitesh Siwach's silver carried perhaps the most remarkable backstory of India's six medallists.A serious knee injury as a teenager kept him away from wrestling for more than 18 months. During that period, he helped his family with its dairy business and sold milk in Panipat.His comeback culminated in an historic Asian Games final appearance in the men's 97kg Greco-Roman category — India's first in the weight class in 64 years.Siwach eventually lost 0-4 to Japan's Yuri Nakazato but returned home with a silver medal and a clear Olympic target."I feel great. This is the first time I am getting such respect and honour. I am experiencing such a great welcome for the first time, and I am very happy," he said. "I had aimed for gold. I didn't win gold, but I did secure the silver medal and I am very happy about that. Since this was my first Asian Games, I am delighted with the silver."Siwach also believes India's Greco-Roman wrestlers can make their presence felt in Los Angeles."People used to say we wouldn't win medals in Greco-Roman, but we will continue to excel. We will bring home medals from the Los Angeles Olympics," he said.His personal target is even clearer."I made some mistakes, which is why I had to settle for silver. My goal going forward is to win gold at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, and I will work extremely hard for it," he added.He has already begun that preparation."My preparation for the Olympics has already begun, starting from the very day I won the medal. I have to bring a gold in the Olympics," Siwach said.Deepak Punia's bronze was another product of perseverance.The 2019 World Championships silver medallist had competed at 86kg and 92kg before moving to 97kg this year following a muscle injury.Despite the challenges of changing weight categories, Punia earned selection for the Asian Games and defeated Mongolia's Gankhuyag Ganbaatar 2-1 in the bronze-medal bout."Winning a medal was quite challenging for me because I used to compete in the 86kg category, but this time I participated in the 97kg category. There were many challenges, and my hope and goal was to win the gold medal. However, I had to settle for the bronze," Punia said.Experience helped him deal with the pressure."I have been playing for a long time, so there is pressure; there is pressure on every athlete. But I understood how I had to handle the pressure. In my mind, it was just that I had to give my best. It was not like I had to take over-pressure. I just had to give my 100 per cent and that's what I did," he said.Antim Panghal also upgraded her medal from bronze at Hangzhou to silver in the women's 53kg category.She lost 1-9 to Japan's Moe Kiyooka in the final after coaches had worked on keeping her calm and confident before the competition."It is my second time winning a medal. But I had thought that I had to come first, but I could not come first. In the future, I will try to do better than this," Panghal said.Sunil Kumar, meanwhile, returned to the podium after knee surgery to win bronze in the men's 87kg Greco-Roman category. He defeated the Philippines' Callum Johnston Roberts 9-0 by technical superiority, becoming the first Indian Greco-Roman wrestler to win two Asian Games medals after his bronze at Hangzhou."I am very happy and want to thank all my fellow countrymen. May your blessings and support continue to be with me," Kumar said.The six medals tell only part of India’s wrestling story in Nagoya.Sehrawat battled through a difficult phase to defeat a reigning world champion. Kalkal stunned an Olympic champion before producing a remarkable comeback for gold. Siwach overcame a serious teenage injury and years of struggle to reach a historic Greco-Roman final. Punia changed weight categories and still made the podium, while Panghal improved her medal colour and Kumar returned from knee surgery to make history.But beyond the six medals was a bigger message — India’s wrestlers are already looking towards Los Angeles.Their words after returning home reflected an ambition that goes far beyond Nagoya: to turn this success into Olympic gold in 2028.
Article Summary: Aman Sehrawat and Sujeet Kalkal struck gold, while Nitesh Siwach and Antim Panghal won silver. Deepak Punia and Sunil Kumar added bronze. India's wrestlers arrived in Aichi-Nagoya carrying questions over injuries, form and confidence. They left with six medals — two gold, two silver and two bronze.

Article Title: From ending South Korea’s reign to booking 2028 LA Olympics quotas: Indian archers return from Asian Games with bigger target
Article Text:
Gold medallist India's Kumkum Anil Mohod, Ankita Bhakat and Kirti celebrate on the podium during the victory ceremony. (Reuters Photo)

‘We proved exactly what they’re made of’

Gold medallists India's Chikitha Taniparthi and Sahil Rajesh Jadhav celebrate after winning the Compound Mixed Team Final. (Reuters Photo)

India's Kumkum Anil Mohod in action. (Reuters Photo)

‘We thought that we would do it, and we did’

India's Kumkum Anil Mohod, Ankita Bhakat and Kirti celebrate after winning the gold medal. (Reuters Photo)

Bigger target: LA 2028

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India's archers returned home from the Asian Games with more than a record medal haul to celebrate. They came back with history rewritten, Olympic qualification secured and the belief that the gap with the world's best is narrowing rapidly.The Indian contingent collected five gold, two silver and two bronze medals in Aichi-Nagoya, with both the compound and recurve squads producing landmark performances. The compound mixed team of Sahil Jadhav and Chikitha Taniparthu secured an Olympic quota place, while the recurve women's team ended South Korea's long-standing dominance by beating the 10-time Olympic champions 5-3 in the final.For a group that had faced questions before the Games, the response was emphatic. India's compound coach Dave Cousins believes the performance should put those doubts to rest.Cousins said the coaching group had deliberately avoided making medal predictions before the Games, instead focusing on preparation and execution.“So early on, they wanted us to make predictions on how many medals we could get. The only thing we were willing to commit to is that our athletes would go prepared and that they would execute the process as best they could,” Cousins said.The results, he argued, were a reflection of a stronger support system around the archers.“When the training is right, the preparation is right and the ecosystem is right, these are the results you get. So we're very happy with that. We're exceptionally happy to clinch the first ever compound archery spot for the Olympic Games. That's a huge thing for us right now,” he added.The success was particularly significant because much of the compound squad was relatively inexperienced on the biggest international stage.“You in the media and the global archery community really had a lot of questions about our younger archers, the new squad. Well, I think we proved exactly what they're made of,” Cousins said.Jadhav and Taniparthu were at the heart of that response. Their mixed-team gold not only delivered another Asian Games title but also secured India's Olympic quota place.Jadhav said the final against Chinese Taipei was less about pressure and more about sticking to a plan repeatedly rehearsed in training.“It feels fantastic, and seeing this grand welcome gives us even more joy. There wasn't pressure as such because we had practised specifically for these situations,” Jadhav said. “It was all about execution, and we delivered. Now I feel all the hard work I've put in so far has truly paid off.”Taniparthu said the victory had given the young group another reason to work harder.“This feels so good and happy, and by this we will get motivated that we have to win more, do more hard work, then every time we will also get this,” she said.The compound women's team also underlined India's growing strength by equalling the world record score during its 238-234 victory over China. Taniparthu won that gold alongside veteran Jyothi Surekha Vennam and Prithika Pradeep.Sahil was also part of the men's gold-medal-winning team, while Ganesh Mani Ratnam Thirumuru won men's team gold and individual bronze. Kushal Dalal was another member of the men's gold-winning side.The recurve contingent produced its own piece of history.Kumkum Mohod emerged as one of India's biggest individual stars, winning women's individual gold and helping the country secure women's team gold and mixed team silver. Her individual triumph also secured an Olympic quota for India.The 17-year-old said the result was the product of collective preparation rather than an individual effort.“What we thought would happen, happened. It was the team's hard work, all the team's motivation, and the support of the Archery Association of India and SAI. That's why everything happened,” she said.In the individual final against South Korea's Oh Yejin, Kumkum consciously shut out the opponent and concentrated on her own shooting.“In the final match, I completely enjoyed my shooting. I held on to my feeling, just shot my arrows and didn't look at who was ahead,” she said.Her advice after the breakthrough was equally simple.“Just stay disciplined and do your best at your work. Don't get carried away. Just keep doing your work properly,” she added.But it was the women's team victory over 10-time Olympic champions South Korea that arguably carried the biggest historical significance. Kirti Sharma was part of the side that defeated the Koreans 5-3, ending their dominance in the event.“India's first gold in this event. We beat Korea to win gold, so this created history for us. I feel very good that I was part of the team that created that history,” Sharma said.The magnitude of the challenge was not lost on the Indian team.“There was pressure because that team always took gold, so there was pressure on us, but we thought that we would do it, and we did,” Sharma said.The men's recurve squad also contributed to India's medal haul, with Dhiraj Bommadevara winning silver in the mixed team event with Kumkum and another silver in the men's team event. Neeraj Chauhan claimed individual bronze and men's team silver, while Yashdeep Bhoge was part of the silver-winning men's team.Bommadevara believes the support structure around Indian archery has changed dramatically.“Earlier, there was hardly any support, and I relied closely on my family and friends. But if it weren't for this government, I wouldn't be standing here today. Our Prime Minister, our Sports Minister and our administrative setup have been so supportive,” he said.The pressure of an Asian Games, he added, was easier to manage because of the team's environment.“Pressure is there for everyone, but we were fortunate to have a team where we could stay cool and calm,” he said.And the next targets are already visible.“Next year, we have the World Championships, where Olympic quotas are there, and after that the LA Olympics,” he said.For Chauhan, the Asian Games was his first experience of the multi-sport event, and the medal made the occasion even more meaningful.“Overall, the experience of the Asian Games was very good. It was my first Asian Games. I went with the hope that I had to bring a medal for India, and bringing this medal has made me and my family very proud,” he said.Bhoge, making his debut, highlighted the collective spirit that helped India navigate the crucial moments.“Obviously it was my debut, so there were crunch moments, but everyone kept their morale up. The team stayed together. Because the whole team stayed together, we were able to play well and maintain ourselves,” he said.The Asian Games medals have therefore brought celebration, but also a bigger expectation. With Olympic quotas secured, South Korea's recurve dominance finally broken and a new generation of compound archers announcing themselves, India's archery programme now has a new benchmark.The Aichi-Nagoya triumph was historic. The next target is bigger — Los Angeles 2028.
Article Summary: India's archers return home from the Asian Games with more than a record medal haul to celebrate. The Indian contingent collected five gold, two silver and two bronze medals in Aichi-Nagoya. The compound mixed team of Sahil Jadhav and Chikitha Taniparthu secured an Olympic quota place.

Article Title: 'It's like water to a thirsty person': Asian Games gold reignites women's hockey at grassroots
Article Text:
